evidence-grounded.why: The criterion holds for every line. Line 1 PASS names wrong builds (a guard returning null or a NaN-coerced value, a guard that only handles undefined) and says why `node -e` catches them: neither prints 0. Its citation "math.js:20" is correct, since line 20 is the reduce/length return. Line 2 PASS names a NaN-safe build that filters out non-finite values, which gives average([NaN,1]) = 1 and is caught. The "|| 0" variant would actually give 0.5, not 1, but it is caught for the same reason. Line 3 FAIL gives two concrete readings: Build A throws a TypeError, Build B returns 0 for null. Line 4 PASS names a build with no test and one with the test in a new file, and both are caught because the line names test/math.test.js. The cited facts check out: the test file imports only add, subtract and multiply; package.json runs `node --test`; and null.reduce does throw a TypeError on the old code.

catches-traps.why: The must_catch item says "Line 2" should FAIL as ambiguous, with two readings named. Counting from 0, line 2 is "average handles bad input sensibly". That is the only vague line. The second line, read 1-based, gives exact inputs and outputs and can't be read as ambiguous, so I took the item to mean the bad-input line. The output marks that line "FAIL". It says the words fix neither which inputs count as bad nor what "sensibly" means. It names two readings: "Build A throws TypeError on average(null)" and "Build B returns 0 for null", and says "Two careful readers will disagree." The wrong_build section makes the same point: the opposite build "also 'meets' line 3 for another reader." So the trap is caught. If "Line 2" was meant 1-based, this would be false, because the output passes that line.

avoids-must-not.why: The must_not list forbids a FAIL on lines 1, 2 or 4. I checked the result for each line in the output. Line 1 ("average([]) returns 0") is PASS. Line 2 (the non-empty list keeps its current results, NaN included) is PASS. Line 4 (the test in test/math.test.js and npm test passing) is PASS. Only line 3, "average handles bad input sensibly", is FAIL. That is allowed, because the list does not mention line 3. The overall "result": "FAIL" comes from line 3 alone and does not mark any forbidden line as failed. Nothing in the output breaks the must_not list.
